questions: Which four subsystems make up an API Connect deployment?

API Connect consists of Management (API Manager, Cloud Manager and the database of APIs, products and subscriptions), Gateway (DataPower API Gateway runtime enforcement), Developer Portal (consumer self-service) and Analytics (API event data).
Correct: these are the four API Connect subsystems.
An APIConnectCluster CR in CP4I deploys all four subsystems together using a chosen profile.
Memorize M-G-P-A: Management, Gateway, Portal, Analytics.
In API Connect, what is a Product?
A package that groups one or more APIs with plans that define access and rate limits, published to a catalog
Products bundle APIs and plans. Consumers subscribe applications to a product plan to get access, and plans define rate limits and approval requirements.
Correct: a product packages APIs with plans for publishing.
A 'Payments' product includes the Payments and Refunds APIs with Bronze (100/hour) and Gold (10,000/hour) plans.
APIs are published in products, never on their own.
What is a Catalog in API Connect?
A publication target, typically one per environment (for example Sandbox, Test, Production), with its own gateway services, developer portal and consumer organizations
A catalog is a staging and runtime environment for products: it is associated with gateway services, optionally a portal site, and holds consumer organizations and subscriptions.
Correct: catalogs are environments for publishing.
A provider organization has Sandbox, Test and Production catalogs; products are promoted between them.
Sandbox is the default development catalog.
What are Spaces in an API Connect catalog used for?
Partitioning a catalog so different teams can independently publish and manage products to the same catalog and portal (syndication)
Allocating disk space to the gateway
With syndication enabled, a catalog is divided into spaces. Each team manages its own products and members in its space while sharing the catalog's portal and gateway.
Correct: spaces enable team-level management within one catalog.
The Retail and Corporate banking teams each own a space in the Production catalog and publish independently to one developer portal.
Syndication plus spaces = multiple teams, one catalog.
Which entity represents an external developer's company that registers applications and subscribes to plans?
Consumer organizations group API consumers (owners and members), their applications (client IDs and secrets) and subscriptions. Provider organizations own and publish the APIs.
Correct: consumer orgs represent API consumers.
Wrong: gateway services enforce runtime policy.
Partner company 'FastShip' has a consumer org with two applications subscribed to the Shipping API Gold plan.
Provider org = API owner. Consumer org = API user.
What is the effect of enabling 'production mode' on an API Connect catalog?
Products must be staged before being published, and conflicts (for example duplicate product versions) are prevented, which supports controlled publishing

Production mode enforces a more controlled lifecycle in the catalog: products must be staged and then published, and conflicting deployments are blocked. It is typically combined with lifecycle approvals.
Correct: it enforces staging and conflict checks.
The Production catalog requires stage and approval before publish; Sandbox allows direct publishing for speed.
Production catalogs: production mode plus lifecycle approvals.
An API product needs a new version that changes the plans, and existing subscribers should move to the new version automatically. Which lifecycle action is MOST appropriate?
Supersede or replace the existing product with the new version, migrating subscriptions as appropriate
Delete the old product, then publish the new one
Publish the new version under a different catalog
Ask every consumer to re-subscribe manually

API Connect supports Replace (moves subscriptions to the new version and retires the old one) and Supersede (deprecates the old version, so existing subscriptions continue but new subscriptions go to the new version), plus subscription migration. These keep consumers working through version changes.
Correct: Replace or Supersede manage version transitions.
Wrong: a different catalog changes the environment, not the version.
Payments v2 replaces v1: all v1 subscriptions migrate to the matching v2 plans in one action.
Replace = move everyone. Supersede = deprecate the old version and steer new subscribers.
What is the difference between 'Replace' and 'Supersede' for an API Connect product?
Replace migrates subscriptions to the new product and retires the old one; Supersede deprecates the old product (existing subscribers keep using it) while new subscriptions go to the new product
Supersede deletes the old product immediately; Replace keeps both active forever
Replace only works in the Sandbox catalog
Replace moves subscribers immediately. Supersede gives existing subscribers time to migrate because the old version stays usable, but deprecated.
Correct: this is the precise difference.
Wrong: replace works in any catalog.
A breaking API change uses Supersede so consumers have 6 months to migrate.
Breaking change -> Supersede (grace period). Compatible change -> Replace.
Which security definition requires API consumers to send the application's credentials (for example an X-IBM-Client-Id header) so the gateway can identify the subscribed application?
An API key security definition (client ID, optionally client secret) identifies the calling application, which the gateway matches to a subscription and plan for rate limiting and analytics.
Correct: the client ID identifies the application and its plan.
A mobile app sends X-IBM-Client-Id; the gateway enforces its Bronze plan limit.
Client ID = application identity. OAuth = user and delegated authorization.
A partner B2B API must authenticate machine-to-machine calls with no end user involved. Which OAuth 2.0 grant type is MOST appropriate?
The client credentials grant lets an application obtain a token with its own credentials when no user is involved, which fits system-to-system B2B integration.
Wrong: authorization code is for user-delegated access.
Wrong: implicit is deprecated and user-based.
Wrong: the password grant is deprecated and user-based.
A logistics partner's server obtains a token with client ID and secret, then calls the shipment API.
No user involved -> client credentials. User delegation -> authorization code (+PKCE).
A single-page web application and a mobile app need users to log in and grant access to their own data through an API. Which OAuth flow is recommended?
Password grant storing user passwords in the app

Public clients (SPAs and mobile apps) cannot keep secrets safely. The authorization code flow with PKCE protects against code interception and is the current best practice; implicit and password grants are discouraged.
Correct: authorization code + PKCE for public clients.
Wrong: deprecated because of token exposure.
Wrong: insecure; apps should not handle user passwords.
The banking app redirects to the bank's login page and exchanges the code (with code_verifier) for tokens.
Public client plus user -> authorization code + PKCE.
An API must accept JWTs issued by the corporate identity provider and reject tokens with invalid signatures or expired claims. Which API Connect assembly policy is used?
The Validate JWT policy verifies the signature (using JWKs or a crypto object) and standard claims such as exp, iss and aud, and rejects invalid tokens before the request reaches the back end.
Wrong: custom code is possible but not the standard approach.
Wrong: rate limiting does not validate tokens.
The gateway validates tokens against the IdP's JWKS endpoint and checks aud=payments-api.
Validate signature, issuer, audience and expiry. All four matter.
Which assembly policy calls a back-end service from an API on the DataPower API Gateway?
The Invoke policy makes the outbound call to the target endpoint (URL, TLS profile, timeout, method). Proxy exists only on the older v5-compatible gateway.
Correct: invoke calls the back end.
API Gateway policies: invoke, map, gatewayscript, validate, ratelimit, jwt-validate...
Consumers receive HTTP 429 Too Many Requests from an API, but the back end is idle. What is the MOST likely cause?
The consumer's plan or assembly rate limit (or burst limit) has been exceeded
429 is returned by the gateway when rate or burst limits defined in the plan (or a ratelimit policy) are exceeded, before calls reach the back end.
Correct: rate limit enforcement at the gateway.
Wrong: that would cause TLS handshake failures.
Wrong: that would cause 503 or connection errors.
A partner on the Bronze plan (100/hour) exceeded its quota; upgrading to Silver resolved it.
429 = throttled by policy, not a back-end failure.
An API call fails at the gateway with HTTP 401 'Invalid client id or secret', but the application exists in the portal. What should be checked FIRST?
Whether the application is subscribed to an active plan of the product (in the same catalog) that contains the API, and whether the correct client ID is sent

The gateway accepts a client ID only if that application has an approved subscription to a plan containing the API in that catalog. Missing or pending subscriptions, the wrong catalog, or a typo in the header cause 401 errors.
Correct: subscription and catalog context are the usual cause.
The app had subscribed in the Sandbox catalog but was calling the Production gateway URL.
401 plus a valid app -> check the subscription, the catalog and approval status.
Why would an architect configure gateway peering for the DataPower API Gateway service in a 3-replica deployment?
So that rate limit counters, token caches and other shared state are synchronized across gateway members, enforcing limits consistently across the cluster

Gateway peering shares data between gateway members, such as rate limit counts, subscription data, token and cache information. Without it, each member enforces limits independently and could permit three times the intended rate.
Correct: peering synchronizes shared gateway state.
With peering, a 1,000/min plan is enforced as 1,000 in total, not 1,000 per gateway pod.
Multi-replica gateways need peering for consistent rate limiting.
A global API platform needs gateways in three regions, central management, and region-local rate limiting with minimal cross-region latency. Which design is MOST appropriate?
One management subsystem with separate gateway services per region (each with local peering), registered to the relevant catalogs, plus region-appropriate analytics and portal placement
A single gateway cluster stretched across all regions with one peering group
Separate API Connect installations with no shared management, copying APIs manually
Route all traffic to one region's gateway

API Connect supports multiple gateway services managed centrally. Keeping peering local avoids cross-region latency in synchronization, while management stays unified. Analytics can be placed per gateway service.
Correct: centralized management with regional gateway services.
Wrong: stretched peering suffers from latency.
Wrong: no central governance; duplicate effort.
Wrong: adds latency and a single region dependency.
EU, US and APAC gateway services all serve the Production catalog; global DNS routes consumers to the nearest one.
Multi-region API runtime = several gateway services, one management plane.
What is the purpose of the API Connect Developer Portal?
Self-service discovery, documentation, application registration and plan subscription for API consumers
The portal (Drupal-based) publishes product documentation and lets consumers sign up, create applications, get credentials, test APIs and subscribe to plans.
Correct: it is the consumer self-service site.
Partners self-onboard: register, create an app, subscribe to Silver, and start calling the APIs in minutes.
Portal = API consumer experience. API Manager = API provider experience.
Which TWO capabilities help enforce API governance and quality in API Connect? (Select TWO.)
Lifecycle approvals for actions such as publish and deprecate in sensitive catalogs
Governance rulesets that scan API definitions for compliance
Allowing direct back-end access bypassing the gateway
Approval workflows control who can change production catalogs. Governance scans validate API definitions against rules (security, naming, documentation).
Correct: rule-based governance checks API definitions.
Publishing to Production needs approval from the API product owner, and governance rules require OAuth on every POST operation.
Governance = rules plus approvals plus audit.
After publishing a new API version, consumers still receive responses from the old implementation. Which is the MOST likely cause?
Consumers are still subscribed to the old product version, which remains published (for example after a Supersede), or they call an old base path or version
Published product versions coexist. Consumers subscribed to the old version, or calling its base path, keep using the old implementation until they are migrated or the old version is retired.
Wrong: published APIs are pushed to gateways.
Migrating subscriptions with Replace moved all consumers to v2.
Version confusion -> check subscriptions and base paths.
What is IBM DataPower Gateway primarily designed for?
Security- and integration-focused gateway processing: traffic control, protocol bridging, XML/JSON threat protection, TLS and policy enforcement

DataPower is a high-performance, security-hardened gateway available as a physical appliance, virtual appliance or container. It enforces security and processing policies on API, web service and messaging traffic.
DataPower enforces mutual TLS and JSON threat protection for internet API traffic before it reaches the internal cluster.
What is the difference between the 'DataPower API Gateway' and the 'DataPower Gateway (v5 compatible)' as API Connect gateway types?
The API Gateway is the modern, higher-performance gateway with native API Connect policies; the v5-compatible gateway exists to run APIs migrated from API Connect v5 that rely on its older policies
The API Gateway cannot enforce OAuth
The DataPower API Gateway is the strategic choice for new APIs. The v5-compatible gateway supports legacy assemblies (for example the 'proxy' policy and older behaviours) during migration.
Correct: API Gateway is modern; v5-compatible is for legacy compatibility.
New APIs target the API Gateway; a handful of migrated v5 APIs stay on v5-compatible until refactored.
Which DataPower objects define the trusted CAs and the certificate and key used when DataPower acts as a TLS client to a back end?
A TLS (SSL) client profile referencing identification credentials (key and certificate) and validation credentials (trusted CAs)
TLS client profiles define outbound TLS behaviour: protocols and ciphers, identification credentials for mutual TLS, and validation credentials to verify the server certificate.
Correct: the TLS client profile with identification and validation credentials.
The backend-mtls client profile presents DataPower's client certificate to the core banking API and validates its certificate against the corporate CA.
Inbound TLS -> server profile. Outbound TLS -> client profile.
DataPower logs 'SSL handshake failure' when calling a back end after the back-end team renewed its certificate with a new intermediate CA. What should be updated?
The validation credentials (trusted CA list) in the DataPower TLS client profile, to include the new intermediate or root CA
If the server certificate chains to a CA not in DataPower's validation credentials, the TLS client rejects it. Adding the new CA chain resolves this.
Correct: trust the new CA chain.
After adding the new intermediate certificate to the validation credentials, calls succeed.
Certificate renewal with a new CA -> update trust stores everywhere.
A legacy partner sends SOAP over HTTPS that must be placed onto an internal MQ queue with no custom code in back-end applications. Which DataPower service is MOST suitable?
A multi-protocol gateway with an HTTPS front-side handler and an MQ back end (or IBM MQ queue manager object)
An XML firewall that writes to Kafka
The multi-protocol gateway bridges protocols: it receives HTTP(S) and can put messages to MQ, with security and transformation policies applied in between.
Correct: the MPGW bridges HTTPS to MQ.
Wrong: not the right service or protocol.
Wrong: it would bring MQ data into Kafka, the wrong direction and protocol.
Partner SOAP orders arrive over mTLS at DataPower and are put to ORDERS.IN for ACE processing.
Protocol bridging at the edge -> multi-protocol gateway.
How is DataPower configuration typically supplied to a DataPower instance in CP4I (DataPowerService)?
Declaratively, through ConfigMaps and Secrets referenced by the DataPowerService CR (domain configuration, local files, certificates), so pods are immutable and reproducible
By logging into each pod's WebGUI and saving manually

In containers, DataPower configuration should be externalized. Domain configuration and local files come from ConfigMaps, and keys and certificates from Secrets, all referenced in the CR. Manual changes inside pods are lost on restart unless exported back to source.
Correct: declarative configuration via ConfigMaps and Secrets.
Wrong: manual changes are not durable or reproducible.
A pipeline exports a domain's configuration from a dev instance into Git and applies it to UAT as ConfigMaps.
Containers are immutable. Configuration must come from source, not from in-pod edits.
Which TWO statements about DataPower high availability in CP4I are correct? (Select TWO.)
Multiple DataPower replicas behind a Service or load balancer provide availability for stateless processing
Gateway peering synchronizes shared state such as rate limits and caches among API Gateway members
A single replica provides HA if it has a PVC
DataPower requires RWX storage for HA

DataPower processing is largely stateless and scales horizontally behind a load balancer. Shared state is synchronized with gateway peering. A single replica is a single point of failure regardless of storage.
Correct: replicas behind a load balancer.
Wrong: one replica is not HA.
Wrong: no RWX requirement for HA.
Three DataPower API Gateway pods spread across zones with peering keep throughput and limits during a zone loss.
Gateway HA = multiple stateless replicas + peering.
Requests to an API pass through DataPower but take exactly 120 seconds before returning HTTP 504/timeout errors. What is the MOST likely cause?
The back end is not responding within the configured invoke or back-end timeout, so the gateway times out
A consistent delay equal to the configured timeout indicates the gateway waited for the back end until the timeout expired.
Correct: back-end latency or unresponsiveness causes a gateway timeout.
Wrong: that fails immediately at TLS.
Wrong: the portal is not in the runtime path.
The back-end database was locked, so every invoke waited the full 120 s timeout.
A fixed-length delay equal to the timeout -> the back end is the bottleneck.
In container deployments of ACE in CP4I, what runs inside each integration runtime pod?
A single integration server (no integration node)
An integration node with many integration servers
A queue manager and an integration node
Containerized ACE runs one integration server per container, independently and without an integration node. Integration nodes are used in traditional VM or on-premises deployments.
Correct: one integration server per container.
Wrong: integration nodes are not used in containers.
Wrong: a local queue manager is not the container model.
Each IntegrationRuntime CR creates pods that each run one integration server hosting the deployed BARs.
Containers = independent integration servers, no nodes.
Which CP4I custom resource deploys ACE flows in recent CP4I versions such as 16.1.0?
IntegrationRuntime is the current CR for running ACE integrations in CP4I. It replaces the older IntegrationServer CR, which is deprecated.
An IntegrationRuntime references BAR URLs and configurations and specifies replicas.
Version detail: IntegrationServer CR (older) -> IntegrationRuntime CR (current).
What is a BAR file in App Connect Enterprise?
A broker archive containing compiled message flows, libraries and resources for deployment to an integration server
A backup of a queue manager
A BAR (broker archive) is the deployable unit for ACE, containing applications, REST APIs, libraries, compiled ESQL, maps and other resources.
A pipeline runs ibmint package to build orders-api.bar from the Git repository.
BAR = what you deploy to ACE.
Which ACE configuration type securely provides credentials (for example database or MQ user IDs and passwords) to an integration runtime?
The setdbparms configuration supplies credentials that ACE uses for database, MQ, HTTP and other resources, stored as a Kubernetes secret behind the Configuration object.
Wrong: policyproject provides policies such as MQEndpoint or JDBCProviders.
setdbparms contains 'odbc::ORDERSDB dbuser dbpass' for the ORDERSDB data source.
Credentials -> setdbparms. Connection settings -> policies. Server settings -> serverconf.
What is the purpose of a policy project (for example an MQEndpoint or JDBCProviders policy) in ACE?
Externalizing connection properties (hosts, ports, queue managers, data sources) so flows can move between environments without code changes
Policies hold environment-specific connection settings. Flows reference a policy by name, and each environment supplies its own policy project configuration.
MQEndpoint policy QMConn points to qm-dev in dev and to qm-prod in production; the BAR stays the same.
Build once, configure per environment through policies.
An ACE flow must read messages from MQ, transform them, and update a database, all in one unit of work. How should it be designed?

MQInput with transactionality enabled (for example automatic for persistent messages), a Compute/Database node update, and global (XA) coordination where needed, so the MQ get and the database update commit or roll back together
Commit the database first and then read the message

ACE flows can run under a transaction. With XA coordination, which in containers depends on the MQ connection setup, the message get and the database update are atomic. Otherwise, design idempotent handling for the window between commits.
Correct: transactional MQInput plus coordinated database update.
Wrong: Kafka does not take part in XA with the database.
If the database update fails, the message is rolled back to the queue and retried, or moved to the backout queue after the threshold.
Atomic message plus database -> transactions or XA, or idempotency if XA is unavailable.
Which ACE artifact type should be used to expose a set of operations defined in an OpenAPI document as a REST API?
A REST API project (built from or generating an OpenAPI definition)
A shared library containing only ESQL
ACE REST API projects implement the operations described in an OpenAPI document. Each operation maps to a subflow, and the API can then be published to API Connect.
Wrong: libraries hold reusable code but do not expose APIs by themselves.
The orders-api REST project implements GET /orders/{id} and POST /orders, and its OpenAPI is pushed to API Connect.
ACE REST API + API Connect = implement + govern.
Which ACE language is a SQL-based procedural language used in Compute nodes to transform and route messages?
ESQL (Extended SQL) is ACE's language for manipulating the message tree in Compute, Filter and Database nodes.
Wrong: KSQL is Confluent's streaming SQL.
Wrong: Rego is the OPA policy language.
ESQL works on the message tree: InputRoot, OutputRoot, Environment, LocalEnvironment.
A flow calls an unreliable HTTP back end. Failures must be retried, and after repeated failures the original message must be preserved for investigation. Which design is BEST?

Use an MQ-driven flow with transactional input: on failure, roll back so MQ redelivers; after the backout threshold, route the message to a backout queue, and add logging in the TryCatch or Catch path
Log the error and delete the message
Retry infinitely in a tight loop
Transactional MQ input gives built-in retry through rollback and redelivery, and backout queues preserve poison messages. TryCatch or Catch handlers record diagnostics.
Correct: rollback-based retries with backout and logging.
Wrong: overloads systems and never gives up.
After 3 attempts (BOTHRESH=3), failed orders move to ORDERS.BOQ, and an operator replays them after the back end recovers.
Retry and poison handling in ACE: transactions + BOTHRESH + BOQNAME + Catch terminal.
An integration runtime in CP4I fails to start, logging 'BIP2241E/policy not found' for an MQEndpoint policy referenced by a flow. What is the MOST likely cause?
The policy project configuration containing that policy was not created or not referenced in the IntegrationRuntime CR's configurations list
The queue manager has too many queues

Flows referencing policies need the policy project deployed, either supplied as a Configuration object of type policyproject that the runtime references, or included in the BAR. If it is missing, the runtime cannot resolve the policy.
Correct: the missing or unreferenced policy project configuration.
Runtime start errors -> check that every referenced configuration exists and is listed.
A containerized ACE flow previously used a local queue manager on the same VM. In CP4I it fails with MQRC 2058/2059 errors. What is the recommended fix?
Configure the runtime to connect to a queue manager as a client (remote default queue manager or MQEndpoint policy with host, port and channel), rather than relying on a local queue manager
Install a queue manager inside the same container
Containerized ACE connects to queue managers over the network as a client. Configure the remote default queue manager or MQEndpoint policies with the correct connection details and credentials.
Wrong: no local queue manager exists.
server.conf.yaml sets remoteDefaultQueueManager to an MQEndpoint policy pointing at qm1-ibm-mq:1414 with channel ACE.SVRCONN.
2059 = queue manager not available. In containers that usually means connection settings are wrong.
Which TWO practices help ACE runtimes in CP4I scale horizontally? (Select TWO.)
Keep flows stateless, or store state externally (for example in MQ, a database or an external cache)
Use multiple replicas of the IntegrationRuntime, optionally with a HorizontalPodAutoscaler
Store session state in the local pod filesystem
Rely on the order of messages across replicas without design
Stateless runtimes can be replicated freely. Replicas plus an HPA add elastic capacity. Local state and assumptions about ordering across replicas break when scaling out.
Wrong: local state is lost or inconsistent across replicas.
Wrong: replicas process concurrently; ordering needs explicit design.
An HPA scales an API runtime from 2 to 10 replicas during a sales event.
Scale-out needs statelessness; ordering needs partitioning or single consumers.
How does a team deliver environment-specific server.conf.yaml settings (for example trace or statistics settings) to an integration runtime without rebuilding the BAR?
Create a serverconf Configuration object and reference it in the IntegrationRuntime CR
Edit the file inside the running pod
Put them in the Kafka topic
The serverconf configuration type provides server.conf.yaml overrides that are mounted into the runtime at startup.
Production serverconf enables flow statistics; dev serverconf enables user trace for debugging.
An integration needs to call a SOAP web service from ACE using a WSDL. Which node is designed for this?
SOAPRequest (or SOAPAsyncRequest) node configured from the WSDL
SOAP nodes use the WSDL to build and parse SOAP envelopes, handle faults, and support WS-Security and WS-Addressing.
Correct: SOAPRequest for outbound SOAP calls.
An ACE flow transforms JSON to the SOAP request defined in billing.wsdl and calls the legacy billing service.
Inbound SOAP: SOAPInput/SOAPReply. Outbound SOAP: SOAPRequest.
Which ACE nodes provide event integration with Kafka topics?
ACE includes Kafka nodes for producing to and consuming from topics, with security settings supplied through policies and credentials.
An ACE flow consumes order events from Event Streams with SCRAM credentials and writes enriched events to another topic.
ACE bridges between MQ, Kafka, HTTP, files and databases.
An HTTP-based ACE flow returns HTTP 500, and the runtime log shows 'BIP2230E' with a database error. What is the BEST next diagnostic step?

Examine the full exception list (BIP messages) to find the innermost error, check data source and credential configuration (odbc.ini or JDBC policy, setdbparms), and enable user trace or flow debug in a non-production environment if needed

ACE exception lists are nested, and the deepest BIP message usually holds the root cause (for example login failed or table not found). Validate the configuration objects that supply connection details and credentials.
Correct: read the nested exception list, then check configurations.
The innermost error was 'SQL30082N security processing failed', so the setdbparms password was outdated.
ACE troubleshooting: always read the innermost BIP message.
A team must guarantee in-order processing of messages per customer while scaling ACE horizontally. Which design is MOST appropriate?

Partition the work by customer key: for example consume from Kafka keyed by customer ID (ordering per partition, one consumer per partition), or use MQ message groups or a dedicated queue per partition so a single consumer handles each key
Increase replicas and rely on MQ's FIFO behaviour across all consumers
Use additional instances on the MQInput node with no partitioning
Order messages afterwards in a database with no keys

Global ordering does not scale. Ordering per key does: Kafka partitions keyed by customer give ordered streams processed concurrently, and MQ supports message groups or per-key routing. Several consumers on one queue break ordering.
Correct: key-based partitioning gives ordered parallelism.
Wrong: competing consumers on one queue break ordering.
Wrong: additional instances process concurrently and break ordering.
Customer events are keyed by customerId into 12 partitions, and 12 ACE consumers each process one partition in order.
Ordering plus scale -> partition by key.
What is the role of the ACE 'Switch server' for callable flows?

It brokers callable flow invocations between integration servers, for example connecting an integration in CP4I to one on premises or in App Connect on IBM Cloud, so flows can call each other across environments
Callable flows let one ACE environment invoke flows in another through a Switch server, often used in hybrid scenarios where cloud integrations call on-premises systems.
Correct: the Switch server routes callable flow invocations.
A cloud-hosted flow invokes an on-premises callable flow that queries SAP behind the firewall through the Switch server and an agent.
Hybrid ACE-to-ACE calls -> callable flows + Switch server.
After scaling an ACE runtime that uses Aggregation nodes from 1 to 3 replicas, some aggregated replies are lost or time out. What is the MOST likely cause?

Aggregation state and reply correlation depend on MQ queues (or state) that must be shared and correctly configured across replicas; replies may be consumed by a replica that does not hold the aggregation context

Stateful patterns such as aggregation or collector need careful design when scaled. Shared MQ-based state on a common queue manager, or session affinity, must be in place, or replies are processed by the wrong replica.
Correct: stateful patterns need shared, correctly configured state.
Moving aggregation state queues to a shared queue manager, configured per the ACE documentation, fixed the lost replies.
Scaling stateful flows -> check where the state lives.
Which App Connect capability helps business users build simple SaaS integrations (for example Salesforce to Slack) with little or no code?
Designer offers a browser-based, low-code experience with SaaS connectors. Flows can run in Designer or be exported to integration runtimes.
An HR analyst creates a flow posting new Workday hires to a Slack channel.
An architect is choosing between baking BARs into a custom image and referencing BAR URLs at runtime for ACE in CP4I. Which statement BEST captures the trade-off?

Baked images give immutability, signing and simple rollback by image digest but need image builds; BAR URLs give faster deployment without image builds but depend on artifact repository availability and credentials at startup
BAR URLs are always more secure
Baked images cannot be used in CP4I
Both are valid. The choice depends on supply-chain requirements, pipeline design and runtime dependencies.
A bank bakes and signs images; a startup uses BAR URLs from Nexus for speed.
An integration runtime pod is Running but not Ready, and the logs show it is still waiting to download and deploy BARs from a slow repository. What is the impact?
The pod does not receive traffic until it becomes Ready; check repository performance or adjust startup and readiness timing
Traffic is sent to it immediately
Readiness gates traffic. If BAR retrieval is slow, readiness is delayed and the startup probe may restart the pod. Fix the repository or adjust probe timings.
Correct: not Ready means no traffic.
Wrong: the readiness gate prevents this.
Moving BARs to an in-cluster repository cut startup time from 4 minutes to 30 seconds.
Slow startup -> check dependencies such as BAR downloads and remote connections.
A flow must convert a fixed-length COBOL copybook record from MQ to JSON. Which ACE capability is designed for this?
DFDL (Data Format Description Language) schema modelling the copybook, parsed with the DFDL parser and mapped to JSON
DFDL describes non-XML and non-JSON formats such as copybooks, CSV and fixed-length records. ACE can import COBOL copybooks into DFDL schemas for parsing and serialization.
An imported copybook DFDL model parses mainframe CUSTREC messages, which a map then converts to JSON.
What does ACE's 'LoopBack' or discovery connector capability primarily enable?
Simplified connectivity to databases and SaaS applications through connectors, without writing low-level code
ACE provides discovery connectors (shared with Designer) and the LoopBackRequest node, which offer model-driven access to SaaS applications and databases.
A flow uses a Salesforce Request node to create accounts without handling the Salesforce API directly.
Connectors reduce custom code for SaaS and database access.

Messages from an MQInput node are repeatedly redelivered and processed, causing duplicate database inserts, and the input queue has no backout queue defined. What is happening, and what should be done?
A poison message causes repeated rollback and redelivery; define a backout queue and threshold (BOQNAME/BOTHRESH) and make processing idempotent
The CPU limit is too low
Without a backout queue, a failing message loops. When part of the work is not transactional, each attempt can cause side effects. Backout configuration plus idempotency stops loops and duplicates.
Correct: configure backout and design for idempotency.
After defining ORDERS.BOQ with BOTHRESH(3) and adding a unique key check, the duplicates stopped.
Repeated processing plus no backout queue = a poison message loop.
Which approach is recommended for unit-testing ACE message flows in a CI pipeline?
Use ACE test projects (JUnit-based) run headlessly with ibmint or the test runner in the pipeline, using recorded or mocked messages
Use Kafka consumer lag as a test
ACE supports flow and node-level unit tests with JUnit-based test projects, which can run in pipelines to validate transformations and logic automatically.
The Tekton pipeline runs the ACE unit tests on each commit before building the BAR.
CI for integrations = automated unit tests plus build plus deploy.
Which ACE node routes a message to one of several outputs based on XPath or ESQL filter expressions?
The Route node evaluates filter expressions and propagates the message to the matching output terminals.
Orders over $10,000 go to the 'approval' terminal; others go to 'auto'.
Route and Filter nodes implement content-based routing.
An ACE REST API must be exposed to partners with OAuth, plans and a portal. What is the recommended integration?
Push or import the ACE REST API's OpenAPI definition into API Connect, configure invoke to the ACE service endpoint, add OAuth security, and publish in a product
Expose the ACE route directly to partners
Use Kafka to expose the API
Use the ACE administration REST API publicly
ACE implements the API, and API Connect governs it. ACE can push API definitions to API Connect, which then fronts the runtime with security and plans.
Correct: ACE implementation plus API Connect governance.
Wrong: dangerous exposure of administrative interfaces.
The ACE orders-api is published as part of the Partner Orders product with an OAuth client credentials security definition.
Never expose admin APIs, and front runtime APIs with a gateway.
API calls via the gateway fail with HTTP 404 'No resources match requested URI'. The back end works. What should be checked?
Whether the API is published to the catalog the gateway URL belongs to, and whether the base path, operation path and HTTP method match the definition
A gateway 404 means no published API operation matches the request path and method in that catalog context.
Correct: check publication, paths and methods.
The client called /v1/order instead of /v1/orders, which is the defined path.
Gateway 404 -> the API was not found in that catalog, path or method.
Which API Connect feature provides visibility into API usage (calls, latency, errors, consumers) for providers and consumers?
The analytics subsystem stores API event records from the gateways and provides dashboards in API Manager and the portal. It can also offload data to external systems.
Product managers view Gold plan usage trends and top consumers on analytics dashboards.
API usage questions -> API Connect Analytics.
A gateway must protect back ends from oversized or deeply nested JSON payloads designed to exhaust parser resources. Which capability is used?
JSON/XML threat protection limits (for example maximum document size, nesting depth and number of properties) enforced by the gateway parser
DataPower enforces parser limits that reject malicious payloads before deeper processing, protecting both the gateway and the back ends.
Payloads over 1 MB or nested deeper than 32 levels are rejected at the gateway.
Threat protection = parser limits at the edge.
A JavaScript-based language for custom processing on DataPower (for example in API Gateway policies or multi-protocol gateway actions)
GatewayScript runs ECMAScript on DataPower for custom message handling, header manipulation and logic beyond the built-in policies.
Wrong: MQSC is MQ's command language.
A GatewayScript policy adds a correlation ID header if the client did not send one.
Prefer built-in policies; use GatewayScript for gaps.
An organization needs internal APIs for employees and external APIs for partners, with different security and visibility, on one API Connect installation. Which design is MOST appropriate?

Use separate catalogs (and gateway services) for internal and external APIs, or product visibility and subscribability settings, with external gateways in the DMZ and internal gateways inside the network
Publish everything to one public catalog
Use only one gateway for both, with no network separation
Separate catalogs and gateway services give clean separation of audience, security and network placement, while product visibility settings control who can see and subscribe.
Correct: segment by catalog or gateway with visibility controls.
The 'Partner' catalog uses a DMZ gateway service; the 'Internal' catalog uses a gateway reachable only on the corporate network.
Audience separation -> catalogs, gateway services and visibility.
Which approach is recommended to connect ACE flows in CP4I to an Oracle database?

Use a JDBCProviders policy (or ODBC configuration) with credentials in setdbparms, supply driver files where needed (for example in a custom image or a generic configuration), and test connectivity per environment
ACE database connectivity is configured through policies (JDBC) or ODBC definitions, with credentials held securely and drivers made available to the runtime.
Correct: policies, credentials and driver provisioning.
A JDBCProviders policy 'OracleOrders' plus setdbparms 'jdbc::OracleOrders user pass' lets a JavaCompute node obtain connections.
Database access in ACE = policy + credentials + driver.
